current_episode.title: The Fast Five: Finding value in high-growth technology companies

guest.bio_context: Richard Brecka has been running Second Alpha Partners for approximately 14 years, building a private equity firm focused on secondary linked investments across IT, media, and telecommunications in North America. He has developed a substantial AI database of private tech companies and S1 filings from the last 15 years to identify investment targets before they reach unicorn status.

context.real_quote: We're a value investor in high growth technology companies, a little bit of both.
key_stats: Typical portfolio company revenue: over 130 million dollars
Typical portfolio company growth rate: over 35 percent
Typical portfolio company age: 10 to 12 years old
Unicorn market concentration: about 70 percent of value in about 25 percent of companies
Liquidity distribution: 99 percent goes to unicorns, 1 percent to pre-unicorn companies
Average secondary discount captured: approximately 60 percent to current market value
Typical stake acquisition per deal: 10 to 15 million dollars, representing about 15 percent of seller ownership
Second Alpha Partners operating history: approximately 14 years
S1 filings database coverage: last 15 years
context.transcript_excerpt: Welcome to the Single Source Podcast, featuring fund managers at the forefront of private markets. We're joined by Richard Brecka, CEO of Second Alpha Partners. Richard, I know you're a private equity firm focused on secondary linked investments, a wide range in IT, media, telecommunications across North America. Please tell us more. What are you investing in? We're investing in a lot of different companies, But what we're looking for is to curate a growth equity stage portfolio of companies in the tech sector and using secondary to get into those late stage companies at a much better value. And so the big theme with Second Alpha is that we're a value investor in high growth technology companies. Typical portfolio company for us is over 130 million of revenue, over 35% growth. They're 10 to 12-year-old businesses, and we're providing liquidity to shareholders in those companies. So value investor, focus and high-growth companies, so a little bit of both. What are the core opportunities or market inefficiencies that Second Alpha is currently targeting? We're buying stock from shareholders in these late-stage companies. When you look at the overall market, the preponderance of value in the companies is in the unicorns. about 70 of the value but in about 25 are sub unicorn which is really where we focus Try to get the companies before they become a unicorn And there a lot of those companies about half the market is sub But when you look at the actual liquidity that's being provided in the marketplace, 99% goes to unicorns. 1% goes to pre-unicorn. And we think there's a better value in capturing those companies before they become unicorns and getting a much better value for our investors by doing that. Yeah, that makes sense. A first mover advantage, so to speak. Why now, though? Why is it an attractive time to deploy this strategy? We've been doing this for about 14 years, and it's been a developing marketplace. When we started, it was somewhat frowned on to have shareholders sell their stock prior to an exit. And we have really built a pretty substantial AI database of all the private tech companies. And we also built a database of all the S1 filings in the last 15 years. And we use that as an inference model to pattern match the private companies that look like companies that filed S1s. And then we target those companies. And so there's a great deal of demand for liquidity. There haven been a lot of liquidity events for a lot of investors And everybody needs money I like the database of the private tech companies That one differentiator But in terms of sourcing and value creation, your approach compared to other PE firms, raising capital on the Apex Invest platform, how do you differentiate yourself? So once we've identified the companies, every year we build a list called the second alpha 200. And those are the companies we want to target during the year. And then we go out and we meet the CEOs of the companies. We talk to them about their business and what their plans are and how they're executing and making sure that that company actually does fit with our model. And once we've figured that out, then we ask the CEO, is there a shareholder that needs liquidity? And the CEO very often says, yeah, there's a guy. and you're not going to want to do this because he doesn't need a lot of money. He needs a million dollars and nobody wants to do that deal. And my answer has always been to the CEO. We'll take care of the guy for you. And the CEO says, if you take care of that guy, I'll give you everything you need to make it happen. And so we get information rights. We get access to management. We get the right of first refusal waived. We get introduced to the seller. we negotiate a deal with him. Usually we only buying about 15 of the seller ownership because we extracting a pretty large discount We average about a 60 discount to current market value And that seller will sell for that because he needs cash. pending_qa.q: How should institutional allocators position secondary equity strategies within diversified portfolio allocations?
pending_qa.r: Allocators can position secondary equity strategies like Second Alpha in multiple ways depending on their portfolio structure. It functions as a growth equity alternative, entering after the last round of growth equity at lower prices. It also generates better multiples on invested capital than traditional LP-led or secondary funds, and can be positioned within late-stage venture portfolios. The strategy represents differentiated exposure to high-growth technology through value investing discipline.
